title: Attention Is All You Need
tldr: Replaces recurrence and convolution entirely with (multi-head) self-attention, yielding a sequence-transduction architecture — the Transformer — that is more parallelizable, trains in a fraction of the time, and sets new single-model state of the art on WMT 2014 translation (28.4 BLEU EN–DE, 41.8 BLEU EN–FR).
contributions: The Transformer: an encoder–decoder architecture built solely from attention and position-wise feed-forward layers — no recurrence, no convolution (Figure 1)
Scaled dot-product attention and multi-head attention, with the 1/√d_k scaling justified by the growth of dot-product variance (Section 3.2, footnote 4)
State-of-the-art WMT 2014 results at a small fraction of prior training cost, plus generalization to English constituency parsing (Tables 2 and 4)
text: Sequence transduction in 2017 was dominated by recurrent encoder–decoders: the encoder walks the input one position at a time, so computation cannot be parallelized within a training example, and long-range dependencies must survive a chain of \(O(n)\) steps (Section 1). Attention had already proven useful for connecting encoder and decoder across arbitrary distances, but only as an add-on to a recurrent core. This paper removes the core. The Transformer keeps the encoder–decoder shape (Section 3, Figure 1) but builds both halves from just two ingredients: multi-head self-attention , which lets every position attend to every other position in one shot, and a position-wise feed-forward network . Order information, previously implicit in recurrence, is injected explicitly through sinusoidal positional encodings added to the embeddings (Section 3.5). The payoff is measured on WMT 2014 machine translation (Section 6.1, Table 2): the big model reaches 28.4 BLEU on English–German — more than 2 BLEU above the best previous results including ensembles — and 41.8 BLEU on English–French, a new single-model state of the art, after only 3.5 days on 8 P100 GPUs. The base model already beats all previously published single models at a training cost of \(3.3\times 10^{18}\) FLOPs, an order of magnitude below competitors. A 4-layer variant also generalizes to English constituency parsing with minimal tuning (Section 6.3, Table 4). The atom of the architecture is scaled dot-product attention (Section 3.2.1, Figure 2 left). Queries and keys of dimension \(d_k\) and values of dimension \(d_v\) are packed into matrices and combined as \[ \mathrm{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \mathrm{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^{T}}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V . \] The \(1/\sqrt{d_k}\) factor is the paper's one delicate choice: if the components of \(q\) and \(k\) are independent with mean 0 and variance 1, the dot product \(q \cdot k = \sum_{i=1}^{d_k} q_i k_i\) has variance \(d_k\) (footnote 4), so unscaled logits push the softmax into regions of vanishing gradient as \(d_k\) grows — which is exactly when additive attention otherwise wins (Section 3.2.1). Scaling restores the fast, matrix-multiply-friendly dot product. title: Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and Translate
tldr: Replaces the encoder–decoder's single fixed-length context vector with a per-target-word context — a softmax-weighted sum of bidirectional-RNN annotations, scored by a jointly trained alignment MLP — which removes the sentence-length bottleneck and brings a single neural model level with phrase-based SMT on WMT'14 En–Fr. This is the mechanism the field now calls attention.
contributions: Diagnoses the fixed-length context vector — not encoder capacity — as the reason RNN encoder–decoder translation degrades on long sentences (§1, Fig. 2).

Introduces a soft, content-based, fully differentiable alignment: each target word gets its own context vector c_i as a softmax-weighted sum of source annotations, trained jointly with the translation model by backpropagation (§3.1, Eqs. 5–6).
Uses a bidirectional RNN encoder so each annotation summarises the sentence around its own position, giving a variable-length source representation that grows with the sentence (§3.2).

Reaches 36.15 BLEU on WMT'14 En–Fr sentences without unknown words, against 35.63 for phrase-based Moses — the first single neural model to match strong SMT, and without Moses's extra 418M-word monolingual corpus (§5.1, Table 1).
Shows the learned weight matrix is directly inspectable and recovers linguistically plausible, non-monotonic alignments (§5.2.1, Fig. 3).
text: By 2014 neural machine translation had converged on one recipe (Sutskever et al., 2014; Cho et al., 2014a): an RNN reads the source sentence into a single fixed-length vector \(c\), and a second RNN unrolls a translation from it (§2.1, Eqs. 1–3). The whole system is one differentiable model trained to maximise \(p(\mathbf{y}\mid\mathbf{x})\), which is elegant — but it forces every sentence, of any length, through the same \(n\)-dimensional pipe. Cho et al. (2014b) had already measured what that costs: BLEU falls off a cliff once sentences run longer than those in the training corpus (§1). This paper's claim is that the bottleneck is the fixed length , not the encoder's capacity, and that removing it takes only a change to where the conditioning comes from. Instead of one \(c\) shared by every output step, the decoder computes a fresh context vector \(c_i\) for each target word , as a convex combination of the encoder's per-position annotations (§3.1). The weights come from a small feed-forward alignment model scored against the decoder's previous state and normalised by a softmax, so the decoder effectively (soft-)searches the source for the positions relevant to the word it is about to emit. Two choices make it work. The alignment is soft — a differentiable expectation rather than a discrete latent variable — so gradients from the translation loss flow straight into the alignment model and the whole system, alignment included, is trained jointly by backprop (§3.1). And the encoder is a bidirectional RNN , so annotation \(h_j\) summarises the sentence with a focus on the words around \(x_j\) rather than only its prefix (§3.2). The source representation is therefore variable-length: it grows with the sentence instead of being squashed into it. On WMT'14 English–French the model (RNNsearch) beats its matched encoder–decoder baseline at every length, and the gap widens with length: RNNsearch-50 shows essentially no degradation out to 50+ words while RNNencdec collapses (Fig. 2). Restricted to test sentences containing only in-vocabulary words, RNNsearch-50\(^\star\) reaches 36.15 BLEU against 35.63 for the conventional phrase-based Moses system (§5.1, Table 1) — the first time a single pure-neural system drew level with strong SMT, and it does so without Moses's additional 418M-word monolingual corpus. title: Multilayer Feedforward Networks are Universal Approximators
tldr: Single-hidden-layer feedforward networks with an arbitrary squashing activation can approximate any continuous function uniformly on compacta and any Borel measurable function in probability — so failures in practice must come from learning, too few hidden units, or noise, never from the architecture class itself.
contributions: Proves single-hidden-layer Σ networks with any squashing function are uniformly dense on compacta in C(R^r) and dense in probability in the Borel measurable functions (Theorem 2.4) — universality with no continuity assumption on the activation.
Establishes the same for ΣΠ networks with any continuous nonconstant activation via the Stone–Weierstrass theorem (Theorems 2.1–2.3).

Shows exact interpolation of any n distinct points by a single hidden layer with n units (Theorem 2.5), and extends universality to multi-output and deeper (l ≥ 2 layer) networks (Corollaries 2.6–2.7).

Frames what universality does and does not buy: nothing about how many hidden units are needed or whether weights can be learned — explicitly deferred to the sieve-estimation and metric-entropy literature.
text: By 1989, feedforward networks were succeeding across applications, but it was an open question whether this reflected a fundamental approximation capability or lucky problem selection. Minsky & Papert had killed the two-layer perceptron two decades earlier; the standing worry was that multilayer networks might also be limited to some special function class (§1). Kolmogorov's superposition theorem was often cited in the networks' defence, but it needs a different , unknown inner transformation for each target function, while practitioners use one fixed squashing nonlinearity (logistic, tanh) and simply add hidden units (§1). This paper settles the question. Using the Stone–Weierstrass theorem plus a constructive reduction through trigonometric polynomials and the Gallant–White "cosine squasher", it proves that a single hidden layer of squashing units — the activation can be any non-decreasing function from 0 to 1, continuous or not — makes the network class dense in the continuous functions (uniformly on every compact set) and dense in the Borel measurable functions in a probability metric, for every input dimension and every input distribution (Theorems 2.3–2.4, §2). The practical reading the authors themselves give (§3): when a network fails, the blame lies with inadequate learning, insufficient hidden units, or a stochastic input–target relation — never with the expressiveness of the architecture family. What the paper deliberately does not address is how many units a given accuracy costs, or how that count scales with input dimension — both flagged as open problems (§3). The objects are function classes built on affine maps.
